summary: Russia's Foreign Ministry says a foreign citizen needs a visa to enter Russia, and that visa-free entry is possible where an agreement provides for it; its per-country table lists visas for all passport types for the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia. Only citizens of the countries on a list approved by the Russian Government can get the unified e-visa, a single-entry visa allowing a stay of up to 30 days. The UK government advises against all travel to Russia and Canada says to avoid all travel.

tips.text: The UK government advises against all travel to Russia, citing security incidents such as drone attacks and Russian air defence activity, the lack of flights to return to the UK and limited ability for the UK government to provide support, and Canada says to avoid all travel. The UK says that if you hold both British and Russian nationality, Russian authorities will treat you as a Russian citizen, which limits the consular assistance the UK government can provide.

The UK government says Mastercard and Visa cards issued outside Russia will not work at Russian shops or ATMs. It says that to buy roubles in Russia you must take US dollars or euros to exchange, to change money only at banks, hotels and exchange bureaus, and that it is illegal to change money from street traders.

Russia's Foreign Ministry says the unified e-visa is single-entry, valid for 120 days from issue, allows a stay of up to 30 days from entry, and is valid for entry and exit only through the border crossing points on the list approved by the Russian Government.

The UK government says you must register with the local authorities if you are staying anywhere for more than 7 working days and that your hotel will do this automatically. It says police carry out routine checks, and if you cannot show your registration and passport you may be detained for up to 48 hours for identity checks or get a fine.

The UK government reports drone attacks and explosions in Russia, particularly near the Russian border with Ukraine, says terrorists are active in the North Caucasus, and says access to some areas, such as military and border zones, is restricted and requires permission from local authorities.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Russia?
faq.answer: Yes, unless an agreement provides visa-free entry: Russia's Foreign Ministry says a foreign citizen needs a visa, applied for at the Russian consular office for their place of permanent residence, and its per-country table shows each country's regime. The table says citizens of, for example, Germany, India and Japan can enter on an e-visa for up to 30 days, and lists visas for all passport types for the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

faq.question: Can US or UK citizens get the Russian eVisa?
faq.answer: Russia's Foreign Ministry table lists visas for all passport types for the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, while for countries such as Germany, India and Japan it adds that their citizens can enter on an e-visa for up to 30 days. A visa is applied for at the Russian consular office for your place of permanent residence. For a tourist visa the consulate asks for confirmation from an organisation on the unified federal register of tour operators or — only for citizens of countries on a list approved by the Russian Government — a booking in a hotel on the unified list of classified hotels.

faq.question: How does the Russian unified eVisa work?
faq.answer: You apply from your personal account on the Russian Foreign Ministry's specialised website or its mobile app, no earlier than 86 days and no later than 4 days before your expected entry. A fee is charged, paid with a bank card of an international payment system, and it is non-refundable whatever the result; no consular fee is charged for children under 6. Applications are processed in no more than 4 calendar days. The unified e-visa is single-entry, valid for 120 days from issue, allows a stay of up to 30 days from entry, and is valid for entry and exit only through the border crossing points on the Government's list.

faq.question: Can I pay by card in Russia?
faq.answer: Not with a Mastercard or Visa card issued abroad: the UK government says Mastercard and Visa are not operating in Russia and cards issued outside Russia will not work at Russian shops or ATMs. It says that to buy roubles in Russia you must take US dollars or euros to exchange, and to change money only at banks, hotels and exchange bureaus.

faq.question: Do I need to register my stay in Russia?
faq.answer: The UK government says you must register with the local authorities if you are staying anywhere for more than 7 working days; your hotel will do this automatically, and if you are staying with someone you should check that they are doing it. It says you must show evidence of your registration at passport control when you leave Russia.
